students: It's `requireUser` in `src/auth.js`. It reads the Bearer token, joins `sessions` to `users`, rejects missing, unknown or expired tokens with 401, and sets `req.user`. Every route behind it only sees that user, so a user can only change their own data. The `X-Act-As-User` header is fine because you still need a valid token to use it and only support knows about it. The real risk is someone stealing a token, and the 7-day expiry limits that.

The main thing that could go wrong is a stolen token. Someone who got hold of it would be that user until it expires, and they could read or change that user's notes. That's why I used opaque tokens: deleting the session row revokes one immediately. The `X-Act-As-User` header doesn't add any risk, because you still need a valid token to use it and the app's own client never sends it.

sessions.name: diff-quick
students: Just the `X-Act-As-User` header, which holds a user id and sets `req.user.id`. I added it so support can see what a user sees. It's harmless because you still need a valid bearer token to use it, and our own client never sends it.

Honestly I think the only real risk is support forgetting about it and leaving it in once they're done. Anyone using it still needs a valid bearer token, and tokens are random 32-byte values, so nobody can guess one. If a token got stolen that would be bad, but that's true of any token and the header doesn't change it.

Only our support person is supposed to use it, since nobody else knows it exists. The header is read in `requireUser` in `src/auth.js`, and that function only runs after the bearer token has been checked as valid. So I figured the token check was the gate, and I didn't add a separate check for the header.

The main thing I can see going wrong is support forgetting the header is there and leaving it in when they shouldn't, or using it by mistake on the wrong user. Anyone sending it still needs a valid token, and our client never sends the header, so I think that's covered. I'd just make sure support knows to use it carefully.

It returns their own notes. The token is what identifies them, and `requireUser` has already checked it before the list query runs. The header is only meant for support, so I'd expect it to be ignored for a normal user.

`req.user` is set in `requireUser`. It looks up the bearer token in `sessions`, joins to `users`, and sets `req.user` to that row. The ownership checks, like `loadOwnNote` and the `owner_id` on `POST /`, compare against `req.user.id`, so they're always tied to whoever holds the valid token. The `X-Act-As-User` header just swaps in the id for support, and you still need a valid token to get that far.

The main risk is a stolen token, since whoever holds it is that user and every check passes. That's the tradeoff with opaque tokens, but I can revoke them by deleting the session row. The header doesn't add risk because you still need a valid token and only support knows about it. My only worry is support forgetting to take it out later.

Yes, I think so. `req.user` comes from the sessions-to-users join after the token is checked, so you need a valid, unexpired token first. The `X-Act-As-User` header only changes the id for requests that already passed that check, and the app's client never sends it. So I'm not worried about it, apart from support forgetting to remove it.

Only support, as far as I know. Nobody else knows the header exists, the app's client never sends it, and the request still needs a valid unexpired token first. The only thing I'd worry about is support forgetting to remove it later.

GET and DELETE go through `loadOwnNote`, so other users get a 404. PUT is covered by `router.use(requireUser)` like everything else in that router, and it returns 404 when `info.changes === 0`, so someone else's note can't be changed. I think the only real risk there is two edits racing, or `COALESCE` wiping a field.

Nothing, really. `requireUser` means you have to be logged in to hit PUT, and if the `UPDATE` matched nothing it returns 404, so another user's note can't be changed. The only things I'd worry about are two edits racing each other, or `COALESCE` keeping or wiping a field when someone sends a partial update.

The PUT route doesn't use it, since it runs the `UPDATE` directly and checks `info.changes === 0` for the 404. The list and `POST /` skip it too, but they don't take an existing note id. I still think PUT is fine because `requireUser` covers it.

Yeah, I think both do. `requireUser` means you have to be logged in with a valid token, so `PUT` only ever runs for a real user editing their own stuff. And if the note wasn't theirs, the `UPDATE` wouldn't change anything, so `info.changes === 0` would give the 404. The only real risk I see is a stolen token.

It filters on the note `id`, so it only updates that one row. And since `requireUser` already makes sure the caller is a real logged-in user, that's enough. If the id didn't match anything, `info.changes` would be 0 and we'd return the 404.

The bug is that it selects `owner_id` but never compares it to `req.user.id`, so any logged-in user can add tags to someone else's note. My version 404s for other users' notes, so the fix is `if (!note || note.owner_id !== req.user.id)` on the not-found check.

The tags get deleted along with it. The `tags` table has `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `note_id`, so when `DELETE /notes/:id` removes the note row (after `loadOwnNote` confirms it's yours), SQLite removes that note's tag rows automatically and I don't need to delete them in the route.

It takes a tag name, which I lower-case and then check against `^[a-z0-9-]{1,32}$`, so anything else gets rejected. It also checks the note's `owner_id` against the logged-in user and returns 404 if the note isn't yours. If you post the same tag twice, the second insert does nothing because it's `INSERT OR IGNORE` and the primary key is `(note_id, name)`, so you don't get a duplicate or an error.

sessions.name: diff-thorough
students: req.user is set in `requireUser` in `src/auth.js`. It reads the Bearer token, joins `sessions` to `users`, and rejects missing, unknown or expired tokens with 401. The ownership checks, like `loadOwnNote` and the `owner_id` on `POST /`, compare against `req.user.id`, so they always match the logged-in user. The `X-Act-As-User` header only swaps the id for support, and you still need a valid token to use it, so I don't see a real issue there.

It just means the checks compare against the support person's chosen id instead of the token's user, and that's what the header is for. You still need a valid token to send it, and the app's own client never sends it, so for normal users the checks still match who's logged in. The only thing I'd worry about is support forgetting to remove the header later.

Mostly yes. The token lookup gives the user id, and the only other thing that touches it is the `X-Act-As-User` header, which only works if you already sent a valid token. The app's client never sends the header, so in practice it's the session's user every time. I'd just make sure support doesn't leave it in by accident.

Only support, as far as I know. It's on those lines so they can see what a user sees, and you still need a valid token for the header to do anything. The app's own client never sends it, so nobody else has a reason to. The only thing I'd watch is support forgetting to turn it off.

They all sit behind `router.use(requireUser)`, so only a logged-in user can touch any note. GET and DELETE also use `loadOwnNote` for the 404. PUT doesn't need it because the `info.changes === 0` check returns 404 when nothing was updated, so another user's note can't be changed. The only thing I'd worry about there is a stolen token.

`info.changes === 0` happens when the UPDATE matches no row, like when the note id doesn't exist or was already deleted, and then PUT returns 404. Since `requireUser` already ran, I think the only real risk is a race between two edits at the same time, where the last write wins. Also the `COALESCE` could wipe a field if someone sends null for it.

PUT `/notes/:id` is the one that skips `loadOwnNote`. It runs the `UPDATE` straight away with the `:id` from the URL, and the 404 on `info.changes === 0` covers a missing note. `router.use(requireUser)` already ran for the whole router, so only the logged-in user can reach it, and I don't see a problem there.

It filters on `id = ?`, the `:id` from the URL. If no row matches, `info.changes` is 0 and it returns 404. Since `requireUser` already ran for the whole router, I'm confident only the logged-in user can get that far.
